content: Users need a video-search application that can query multiple websites at once for streaming sources and downloadable video listings. A user should be able to search for a specific title or genre, choose which types of sources to include, compare organized results, and retain useful favorites. System maintainers also need a way to control which external sites participate in searches.

People usually want this when they already know what they’re looking for, but they don’t want to check ten sites one by one. That could be a specific title, a series, or even a genre when they’re browsing and comparing what’s available across streaming and download sources.
They’re usually trying to save time, find the best available source, and compare results in one place so they can pick the most useful or reliable option. Some users also want to keep track of favorites for things they return to often, rather than searching from scratch each time.

They’re usually trying to make a decision, not just collect a list of links. In practice, they want to quickly compare what’s available, filter out the source types they don’t care about, and end up with the best option for watching or downloading.

I’d keep it broader for now. “Comparing sources to choose the best watch-or-download option” sounds right as a common case, but I don’t want to lock us into that as the only intent until we’ve checked with a few more users or stakeholders.

Ideally it should let them pick up where they left off. If a favorite came from a search with certain filters or source preferences, I’d expect the system to preserve that so they can rerun it or reopen the same result set quickly. Showing the saved item directly is useful too, but I think keeping the original search context is the more important part.

We want it focused on legitimate external sites that provide streaming sources or downloadable video listings, not just any random content on the web. Yes, there should definitely be exclusions, especially if a site is unreliable, broken, or not approved by the maintainers, and I’d also expect us to avoid anything that violates policy or licensing concerns.

At minimum, the user should be able to enter a title or a genre, and if they paste something more descriptive like a full phrase, the system should still try to interpret it sensibly. Before running the search, I’d expect the app to clean up obvious formatting issues, trim extra spaces, and probably normalize the text so search across multiple sites is more consistent.

I don’t think we’ve defined a hard minimum yet, and I’d be cautious about setting one too early. My expectation is that results should be relevant enough to the query and then be sortable or filterable, but the exact threshold probably needs testing because different sites will vary a lot in how they describe the same content.

It needs to work reasonably well under normal internet conditions, but I’d expect variability because the external sites will not all respond the same way every day. The app should stay usable if one source is slow or temporarily unavailable, and it should probably return partial results instead of failing the whole search.

Web first would make the most sense. That gives us the fastest path for users to search from anywhere, and it also keeps the maintainers’ control over external sites centralized instead of spreading it across different client apps.

We should support the major current browsers and make sure it works well on both desktop and tablet-sized screens at minimum. I don’t think we need to optimize for very old devices in the first version, but it should still remain usable if performance is a bit limited.

Ideally, the first useful results should start showing within a few seconds, even if the full aggregation is still coming in. I wouldn’t want users waiting too long for the whole search to finish, but some delay is acceptable if we can show partial matches quickly and keep the interface responsive.

I don’t have a firm number yet, so that would need to be confirmed with the team. For the first release, I’d expect it to handle a modest public load comfortably rather than very high traffic, but I can’t give you a reliable peak count without checking expected adoption.

For the first release, I’d plan for low to moderate concurrent public use, enough that a small crowd can search at the same time without the service feeling sluggish. I can’t give a precise number yet, but I’d want it sized more like an early public web app than a high-scale consumer platform.

Yes, I’d expect some basic cleanup so the search is forgiving. We should probably ignore extra punctuation and spacing, and handle simple plural or singular variations so users don’t have to type the exact form. Quoted phrases should likely stay more exact, especially when someone is searching for a specific title.

In day-to-day discussions, I’d probably call them search sources or providers when talking about the external sites, and then separate them into streaming sources versus downloadable listings. For the user-facing side, I’d still refer to those as results or matches, depending on whether they’re organized by title, genre, or source type.

Yes, we’d want to prefer the most direct and reliable reference we have for each result, so if a source gives both a listing page and a deeper access link, we should use the one that actually gets the user to the playable or downloadable item. If that primary reference is missing or clearly broken, then falling back to the listing page is better than dropping the result entirely.

From a business point of view, user accounts and saved favorites should be protected with standard login security and stored securely, and admins should have a clearly separate level of access from regular users. I’d expect role-based permissions so only maintainers can change which sites participate in searches, and we should keep an audit trail for those changes. Beyond that, I don’t have a special policy in mind yet, but I’d want the usual basics like encrypted transport and careful handling of any stored user data.

The primary role is a regular end user who wants to search across multiple video sites, filter by source type, and review the results in one place. Admin or maintainer users are secondary, mainly for managing which external sites are included.

I’d want it remembered as a saved default, because most users will probably stick with the same source types most of the time. But they should still be able to override it for a single search if they want to broaden or narrow the results.

It should apply only to the current search, not replace their saved default automatically. If they want to change their default, that should be a deliberate action in their settings so they don’t lose their usual preference by accident.

I’d prefer the system not hide it automatically, because users may still want to inspect the source. It should be clearly labeled as a weak or possibly inaccurate match, and users should be able to ignore it or remove it from their own view if they don’t want to see it again.

If the direct access link is broken, I’d want the system to keep the listing page available as a fallback if that’s all we have. At the same time, it should clearly show that the direct link failed or is unavailable, so the user isn’t misled into thinking it’s playable right away.

They should be able to manage that from an admin screen, probably by turning sites on or off in a controlled list. I’d expect each site to have basic status info there too, so maintainers can see what’s active, what’s disabled, and maybe any notes about why.

By default, searches should run across all enabled sites so users get the broadest coverage without extra setup. But users should definitely be able to narrow it to a chosen subset when they want more focused or faster results.

I don’t think we have a hard business rule for that yet. My expectation is that the results should be organized by relevance and source type, not by which site was searched first, unless there’s some technical reason to favor one site over another.

They should still be shown if they have some plausible relevance, but lower in the results so the stronger matches come first. If something is extremely weak or clearly off-topic, then it should probably be omitted rather than cluttering the list.

It should stop being used immediately for new searches once it’s disabled. I’d still want any existing user session to keep whatever results it already has, but the site itself shouldn’t keep participating in fresh queries until a maintainer re-enables it.

A useful favorite would be a result that gives the user a clear path back to the content later, so it should have at least a recognizable title and a working destination link. If we can capture the source site, format, and maybe a thumbnail or brief description, that would make it more useful, but the title and link are the minimum.

Yes, I think notes and tags would be useful. Tags should probably be simple freeform labels, but with some basic limits so they stay manageable, and notes should be short text rather than a full comment field. I don’t know the exact limits yet, but I’d expect us to prevent anything that makes favorites messy or hard to search later.

Duplicate tags should be collapsed so the same label doesn’t get added twice, and overly broad tags are okay as long as they’re still meaningful to the user. I’d expect notes and tags to stay editable after saving, with no special restriction except that changes should update immediately and not break the favorite itself.

If the underlying video result has changed or disappeared, the user should still be allowed to edit or remove their favorite, but we should warn them that the original source may no longer be valid. Removal should probably always be straightforward, while edits that depend on live metadata might need a refresh or confirmation if the content has drifted.

Yes, those notes and tags should travel with the favorite when it’s copied or moved, because they’re part of how the user recognizes it. If it’s shared, I’d expect the notes and tags to be included only if the user chooses to share that metadata, since some notes might be personal and not meant for everyone.

Personal notes should be treated as private by default, so they shouldn’t be exposed to other users unless the owner explicitly shares them. Tags are a little more flexible, but if they’re tied to a private collection or personal organization, they should stay visible only to the owner unless we define a deliberate sharing option.

Disabling should remove it from fresh queries right away, because that’s the point of the control. I can imagine an exception only if there’s some emergency override for admins, but normally once it’s disabled, new searches should stop using it until it’s re-enabled.

That should be limited to a small maintainer or administrator group, not general users. I’d expect it to be used only for operational emergencies, like validating a fix or handling a temporary outage where someone needs to test the integration before fully re-enabling it.

It should live inside a dedicated admin area rather than alongside the normal user search experience, so it’s clearly separated. Only authenticated maintainers or admins should be able to reach it, and regular users shouldn’t even see a link to it.

It should show a very clear disabled status, like a red or muted label, so it stands out immediately from active sites. I’d also want the last disabled time and maybe the reason or note from the maintainer, because that helps someone decide whether it’s safe to re-enable.

From a business perspective, onboarding a new source needs to make sure the site can participate in searches with the right source type, availability, and rules without breaking the rest of the catalog. If there’s an existing configuration to migrate, the maintainer should be able to see a before-and-after summary or validation result so they know the important settings were carried over correctly.

It should flag anything that could change how results are grouped, labeled, filtered, or ranked, because those are the things users will notice most. If a setting is missing or mapped differently, the summary should say whether it was carried over automatically, left blank, or needs manual review before the source is enabled.

Yes, definitely. If a rule doesn’t apply to the new source type, or a setting is intentionally omitted because there’s no equivalent, the summary should call that out explicitly instead of treating it like a successful carryover. And if a change affects search behavior materially, I’d expect it to be held for approval before the source is allowed into aggregation.

If the favorites still point to the same logical title or item, I’d want them carried over so users don’t lose useful saved content. If the new source type can’t match them reliably, then they should be left behind or flagged for review rather than guessed, because a bad favorite is worse than none.

It should be marked for user review rather than quietly hidden, so someone can understand why it didn’t come across. If the item becomes matchable again later, I’d like there to be a recovery path so the favorite can be re-associated instead of forcing the user to recreate it.

Overrides should be limited to a very small admin group and require stronger authentication than normal use, like a recheck or step-up confirmation. I’d also want every override logged with who did it, when, what was changed, and why, since emergencies are exactly when we need a clean audit trail.

Yes, I’d want success or failure captured, along with the specific source or external site affected and any resulting state change. It would also be useful to record whether a follow-up review, alert, or rollback was triggered, because that helps us prove the override was handled properly after the fact.

If the intended outcome wasn’t fully achieved, I’d treat it as a failure even if something changed along the way. Partial changes should be noted in the log, but success should really mean the override completed cleanly and left the source in the intended state.

Yes, I’d expect at least an alert for any failed or partial override, especially if it touches a live source or search behavior. If the change affects multiple sites or could impact users broadly, then it should also trigger a follow-up review so someone can confirm the system wasn’t left in an inconsistent state.

Normally the maintainer or admin group should own making the change, and a product or operations owner should approve and validate it before it goes live. If the update affects a lot of users, changes how results are ranked or filtered, or touches a sensitive external source, then I’d expect additional sign-off from whoever is responsible for risk or operations.

Favorites should be tied to the user account and persist across sessions, and ideally across devices if the user signs in. I don’t think they should disappear on their own unless the underlying item is no longer usable, though in that case we’d keep the favorite but mark it as unresolved until it can be matched again.

I’d keep it in the user’s favorites for a while rather than deleting it automatically, because users may want the record of what they saved. If it stays unresolved for a long time, it could be moved into an inactive or stale state, but I wouldn’t remove it without some user action or a clear retention rule from the team.

It should still be visible in the main favorites list, but clearly flagged as unresolved so the user knows it’s not currently usable. I wouldn’t hide it by default because that would make it too easy to lose track of something they saved intentionally.
